newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-Buba fosters confusion to break mark's fall.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Buba fosters confusion to break mark's fall.

text.p: Germany's Bundesbank, an established master of suspense, kept financial markets hopping this week.
Conflicting policy views from top officials at the powerful central bank forced swings in market sentiment on how, if at all, it would act to support its struggling deutschemark.
The uncertainty which has reigned since July 24, when the Bundesbank decided to leave open its options on setting short-term interest rates, found little relief.
Instead, attention has been catapulted forward to Tuesday, when the next repo rate -- the Bundesbank's main money market rate -- will be set.

"We have been left with the classic Bundesbank ability to keep us guessing," said David Brickman, European economist at Yamaichi International in London. "And that is exactly what the Bundesbank wants markets to do."
The bank, which has in its statute a primary responsibility to protect the national currency, is clearly annoyed by the mark's relentless decline and may be fostering confusion to break its fall.
"When the dollar was at 1.70 marks we said the correction was over and that the dollar was in an area that would like to see," council member Ernst Welteke told German radio on Friday.

The dollar, having taken little notice of the warnings back then, made a perfunctory bow to an early low of 1.8625 marks, but soon recovered, turning its attentions to further words from Welteke suggesting a monetary tightening was not imminent.

"As long as we see no clear sign of climbing inflation we should not change interest rates," Welteke said, adding that Germany's stinging jobless levels and weak growth meant it would not be appropriate "to turn the interest rate screw".

But his remarks jarred against earlier comments this week from Bundesbank chief economist and directorate member Otmar Issing, who pointed to rising capacity utilisation and a "booming" export sector as proof that the German economy is not as vulnerable as some might think.
"The economy is not exactly overheating, but it should not be labelled worse than it is," Issing said.
The Bundesbank officials offered few favours for financial markets looking for a quiet start to the August holiday period.

A blaze of speculation that the Bundesbank might indeed allow money market interest rates to drift higher by setting a variable rate agreement next Tuesday was fanned by Issing at the beginning of the week, and all but extinguished by Welteke before the weekend.

Some analysts said the conflicting comments showed the Bundesbank was struggling to find a way out of a tight corner, aware that interest rate rise would be unpopular in Europe and dangerous for the economy, but equally aware that "verbal intervention" is weak ammunition against a currency slide.
Others, however, said the central bank's confusing utterences were carefully engineered -- and having the desired effect.

Yamaichi's Brickman said that if the central bank signalled a rate rise was definitely on the cards, the risk of a slide in debt prices and a consequent racheting up of market interest rates would have been too great.
On the other had, a strong hint that no rate rise is imminent would have given currency traders free rein to chase the mark even lower, he added.

With markets continuing to hop from one leg to the other on whether the Bundesbank will or won't move the repo, the mark has been topped and tailed relatively well this week, trading in a range from 1.85 to 1.89 marks to the dollar.

And despite Welteke's determined repetition that the 1.70 mark-level -- a rate currency markets abanboned at the end of May -- was a dollar "in an area that would like to see", analysts said the key factor for the Bundesbank was not the mark's level, but the pace of its deterioration.

"The Bundesbank is worried about the momentum of the mark's fall more than about its absolute level," said Ralf Kugelstadt, economist at UBS in Frankfurt. "The bank is not interested in getting the dollar back down to 1.70 marks."
